prompt.context: Our client, UK-based Magic Media, is participating in an auction for the rights to broadcast the 2016 Quiddich World Cup. Magic Media is a mature company that derives the vast majority of its revenues from selling TV advertisements.
prompt.question: What should we bid on the broadcasting rights? What factors will affect our bid?

clarifying_info.q: Who are the competitors in the auction?
clarifying_info.a: Magic Media has 3 competitors: 2 smaller US-based players looking to boost their international presence (likely with higher production costs and possibly lower ad revenues, and may be willing to loss-lead), and 1 large UK-based player that is a mature company with similar economics to Magic Media.

clarifying_info.q: How long does the World Cup last and what is the broadcast schedule?
clarifying_info.a: The 2016 Quiddich World Cup lasts 3 weeks. It begins with an opening ceremony on a Sunday afternoon and ends with the final match and closing ceremony on a Saturday evening. Magic Media can broadcast 6 hours per weekday and 8 hours per weekend day, plus an extra 2 hours on ceremony days to allow for the length of the ceremony.
Heavier viewing is expected during weekday evenings (the last 2 hours of each weekday), all weekend days, and peak viewing during the final day of games and the two ceremonies.
Due to complicated logistics, Magic Media will need to spend an extra $10M to produce the broadcast over normal programming.

Magic Media can show ads for no more than 10 minutes per hour. They charge double their normal rates for the World Cup: $50K/min for non-prime time, $200K/min for prime time, and $500K/min for peak time. Normal rates are $25K/min, $100K/min, and $250K/min respectively.

clarifying_info.q: What interest rate or cost of capital should we use?
clarifying_info.a: Make a reasoned assumption. A rate of 10% is reasonable.

framework: Determine marginal TV revenue from broadcasting the World Cup
Calculate total broadcast hours by category (peak, prime, non-prime) based on tournament schedule
Apply advertising rates and 10-minute-per-hour cap to estimate gross revenue
Account for the fact that only marginal (incremental) revenue counts — use half of gross revenue as marginal
Deduct incremental production costs ($10M) to arrive at marginal profit
Discount marginal profit to present value given the 5-year gap between auction payment and broadcast receipts
Assess competitor bidding behavior to determine optimal bid below but close to present value

questions.prompt: What are the key issues we need to examine before determining our bid?
questions.guidance: A strong candidate identifies four key dimensions: (1) calculating marginal TV revenue from the broadcast; (2) understanding broadcast hours and ad rates by time category; (3) accounting for the time value of money since payment is now but receipts are in 2016; (4) understanding competitor economics and bidding strategy to set a strategically optimal bid.

questions.prompt: Calculate the total number of peak, prime, and non-prime broadcast hours over the tournament.
questions.guidance: Tournament lasts 21 days total: 15 weekdays, 5 normal weekend days, 1 final match day. Opening ceremony is on a Sunday (weekend + 2 extra hours = 10 hours), closing ceremony is on a Saturday (weekend + 2 extra hours = 10 hours but this is the final day). Final match day = 8 + 2 = 10 hours. Peak hours = hours for final match day + opening ceremony + closing ceremony = 10 + 2 + 2 (just the ceremony portions) OR more directly: peak = 12 hours total across the 3 special days. Prime hours = last 2 hours of each of 15 weekdays (30 hours) + all 5 normal weekend days × 8 hours (40 hours) = 70 prime hours. Non-prime hours = first 4 hours of each of 15 weekdays = 60 non-prime hours.

math.setup: Tournament = 21 days: 15 weekdays, 5 normal weekend days, 1 final match day (Saturday with closing ceremony); Opening ceremony on Sunday (weekend day with +2 extra hours)
steps: Peak hours: final match day hours + opening ceremony hours + closing ceremony hours = 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 hours (ceremonies/final are peak; the casebook gives total of 12 peak hours)
Prime hours on weekdays: 2 prime hours/weekday × 15 weekdays = 30 prime hours
Prime hours on normal weekends: 8 hours/weekend day × 5 weekend days = 40 prime hours
Non-prime hours: 4 non-prime hours/weekday × 15 weekdays = 60 non-prime hours
math.answer: 12 peak hours, 70 prime hours, 60 non-prime hours

questions.prompt: Calculate total gross advertising revenue and then marginal profit from broadcasting the World Cup.
questions.guidance: Apply the 10 min/hr ad cap and the doubled rates to each hour category. Total revenue = sum across all three tiers. Marginal revenue = total revenue / 2 (since these are incremental revenues over normal programming). Marginal profit = marginal revenue minus $10M extra production costs. Strong candidates may also note that spillover viewership onto normal programming could increase marginal revenue by $2.5M–$10M.

math.setup: Ad revenue = hours × 10 min/hr × rate per min. Rates: peak $500K/min, prime $200K/min, non-prime $50K/min. Marginal profit = (total revenue / 2) − $10M extra production cost.

questions.prompt: The World Cup takes place in 2016 but the auction is this year (2011). How much is the future stream of revenue worth today?
questions.guidance: Candidates must recognize the time value of money: Magic Media pays for the license now but receives ad revenues 5 years later. They should apply a discount rate (10% is a reasonable assumption if the candidate needs prompting). PV = marginal profits / (1 + r)^n.

math.setup: PV = Marginal Profit / (1 + Cost of Capital)^Years. Marginal Profit = $105M, Cost of Capital = 10%, Years = 5.

brainstorming.prompt: What risks and strategic considerations should Magic Media weigh when setting its actual bid?

categories.name: Competitor dynamics
ideas: The large UK competitor has similar economics — they will likely value the rights at a similar PV, so bidding close to $65.2M is competitive
The two US-based players may loss-lead to gain international presence, creating upward pressure on bids
Understanding past bidding behavior of the UK competitor is important — are they known to underbid to capture surplus?
More competitors increase uncertainty and make underbidding more risky

categories.name: Revenue risk
ideas: Ad inventory may not sell out — insufficient advertiser demand at the premium rates would reduce revenues
Ratings and viewership could disappoint, reducing the premium advertisers are willing to pay
Spillover viewership onto normal programming could add $2.5M–$10M in additional marginal value

categories.name: Bid strategy
ideas: Bidding at full PV ($65.2M) is acceptable since it meets the cost of capital
Bidding below PV captures surplus but risks losing the auction
An overly optimistic model (ignoring downside risks) makes a bid at full value risky
Underbidding is less attractive when loss-leading competitors are present

recommendation: Magic Media should bid below but close to the projected present value of $65.2M
A bid at value is entirely acceptable because it produces profits that meet the cost of capital
risks: Revenue projections could be too optimistic if advertiser demand is insufficient to fill all time slots at premium prices
The model could be overly optimistic if downside scenarios (low ratings, weak demand) are not accounted for
The two US-based competitors may loss-lead, driving the winning bid above Magic Media's rational value
Over- or under-bidding due to insufficient understanding of competitors' positions
next_steps: Research past bidding behavior of the UK competitor to calibrate their likely bid
Develop a downside revenue scenario to stress-test the $65.2M valuation
Assess whether the US competitors' strategic motivations could push bids materially above $65.2M
Consider whether spillover viewership upside ($2.5M–$10M) justifies a slightly higher bid ceiling
